title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 4: Gravely Abusive Contracts
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address to the Employers Confederation of the Philippines explaining why the Supreme Court voided three mega-contracts, answering the criticism that the Court 'is interfering inordinately in economic matters, specifically in nullifying billion-peso contracts entered into by the government.'

The constitutional premise: the Constitution gives the judiciary 'the duty - not just the power or authority - to strike down any act of any agency or instrumentality of government' tainted with grave abuse, so that once abuse is shown the courts 'have no choice but to invalidate it as a matter of constitutional duty.'

A case-by-case account of the AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA PACIFIC Decisions showing 'exactly how and where grave abuse of discretion lies' -- unconstitutional conveyance of reclaimed and submerged land, bidding rules violated and contracts altered after award, and an election automation contract awarded to an entity that had not bid, with machines that had failed the technical tests.

The business-facing conclusion: by invalidating these contracts the Court upheld the rule of law as 'an essential ingredient of economic governance' and signalled that government contracts must be entered into fairly and evenhandedly -- far from an 'unwanted interloper,' it defended 'the leveling of the playing field.'
sub_topics: He opens with the September 11, 2003 courtesy call of the US-ASEAN Business Council on the Supreme Court, where Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. asked him, as chairman of the Committee on Public Information, with Justices Antonio T. Carpio and Adolfo S. Azcuna, to receive the visiting American investors.

Asked what advice would safeguard their investments, he answered that justices normally do not render advisory opinions: under the adversarial system judges are 'passive participants,' speaking mainly through decisions that must 'always be understood in the context of their peculiar facts.'

He identifies four contracts he was asked by ECOP president Rene Y. Soriano and organizing chairman Feliciano L. Torres to discuss -- AMARI, PIATCO, MEGA PACIFIC and the Western Mining Company case -- and sets the fourth aside as sub judice, since a Motion for Reconsideration was pending and he had written the main Dissenting Opinion.
He defines the standard: grave abuse of discretion exists when an act is done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence, or when it is executed whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily.

AMARI: the 1995 Joint Venture Agreement with the Public Estates Authority covered the 157-hectare 'Freedom Islands' plus 250 hectares of submerged land; in 1998 former solicitor general Francisco Chavez sued, and the Court, unanimous at 13-0 through Justice Carpio, held that reclaimed lands are alienable public domain that may be leased but not sold to private corporations, while submerged areas are inalienable and outside the commerce of man.

The May 6, 2003 Resolution clarified that reclaimed alienable land sold to a public or municipal corporation becomes patrimonial property that may be resold to private parties -- a clarification that 'quieted the anxieties' of companies that had bought reclaimed real estate from Pasay City.

The November 11, 2003 Resolution, citing two Senate committee investigations, found land near Roxas Boulevard conveyed at P1,200 per square meter against a market price of P90,000 -- a difference of P140.16 billion, 'equivalent to the budget of the entire judiciary for seventeen years,' closing what he calls 'the grandmother of all scams.'

PIATCO: the 1997 Concession Agreement for NAIA Terminal III under the BOT Law was amended in 1998 and supplemented three times without public bidding; in a Decision by Justice Reynato S. Puno the Court ruled 10-3-1 that MIAA had gravely abused its discretion.

The five PIATCO defects: an award to a bidder that failed the financial requirement; an amended agreement substantially different from the one bidded out, nullifying the 'fair competition essence'; a government obligation to pay PIATCO's creditors in breach of the BOT Law's ban on 'government guarantees in any form'; payment obligations on emergency takeover contrary to Section 17 of Article XII; and an exclusive right to operate a Luzon international passenger terminal that transgressed the constitutional prohibition against monopolies.

The January 21, 2004 Resolution stressed that bidding must follow the prescribed terms and parameters, that after award 'all that is left to be done by the parties is to execute the necessary agreements and implement them,' and that otherwise 'public bidding becomes a mockery.'

MEGA PACIFIC: in a Decision he wrote, the Court voted 9-5 to invalidate the Comelec automated counting machines contract awarded 'in inexplicable haste' and in reckless disregard of Comelec's own rules.

The MEGA PACIFIC defects: the award went to 'Mega Pacific Consortium,' which had not bid, while the contract was signed with 'Mega Pacific Solutions, Inc.,' which had bid but was ineligible; the machines flunked the DOST tests and the 99.9995 percent accuracy requirement, watering down standards after award being 'a sure indication of fraud'; the software could not detect previously downloaded precinct results, so 'election fraud could be perpetrated on a massive scale'; and the machines could not print the audit trail without data loss.

Aggravating the failures, Comelec admitted the software tested was merely a 'demo' version, prompting the Court's question of what the point was in awarding a bid when the software 'was still to be created by the winner,' having awarded the contract 'without having seen, much less evaluated, the final product being purchased.'

The epilogue of that Decision framed the case as bearing on Comelec's very capacity to conduct honest elections, the abusive acts having put in jeopardy 'the pith and soul of democracy - credible, orderly and peaceful elections.'

He closes that although some businessmen who entered these void contracts 'may have suffered some losses,' business in general was advanced, and quotes the Mega Pacific Decision that public bidding aims to level the playing field so that each bidder bids under the same conditions.

stances.claim: Justices should not give advisory opinions, because under the adversarial system judges are passive participants who speak through decisions rendered only after meticulously hearing the parties.
stances.rhetorical_move: declining the question asked, then explaining the institutional reason for declining it

stances.claim: Once a government act, order, directive or contract is shown to have been gravely abused, the courts have no choice but to invalidate it, because the Constitution imposes a duty and not merely a power.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty framing -- removing judicial discretion from the question of whether to intervene

stances.claim: The AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA PACIFIC contracts were each entered into with grave abuse of discretion, in violation of the Constitution, the bidding laws and the agencies' own rules.
stances.rhetorical_move: case-by-case forensic walkthrough, enumerating each defect with quotations from the Decisions

stances.claim: Far from being an unwanted interloper in economic matters, the Court in these Decisions promoted business by upholding the rule of law, stability, rationality and transparency, even if particular businessmen lost money.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing the criticism -- losses to some contractors set against gains to business in general

notable_anecdotes: American business leaders of the US-ASEAN Business Council called on the Supreme Court on September 11, 2003, and during the open forum asked what advice the justices could give to safeguard their planned investments.
He declined to advise them, explaining that judges are passive participants who speak only through decisions understood in the context of their peculiar facts.
He excuses himself from discussing the Western Mining Company case because it was still sub judice and he had filed the main Dissenting Opinion in it.

He recounts the P140.16 billion price gap in the AMARI reclamation -- P1,200 versus P90,000 per square meter -- measured by the Court as the entire judiciary's budget for seventeen years and 'more than three times the Marcos Swiss deposits.'

He recalls Comelec's admission that the software it had tested was merely a 'demo' version while the final version was still being developed, and the Court's question of why the machines were bought and paid for at all.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' presents CJP's address to the Employers Confederation of the Philippines on why the Supreme Court had voided three mega-contracts. He opened with the courtesy call of the US-ASEAN Business Council on September 11, 2003, when visiting American investors asked what advice would safeguard their investments and he replied that justices normally do not render advisory opinions, since under the adversarial system judges are passive participants who speak through decisions tied to their peculiar facts. He read that polite question as the familiar criticism that the Court was interfering inordinately in economic matters, and took up the AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA PACIFIC Decisions, setting aside the Western Mining case as sub judice because he had written the main dissent. His premise was that the Constitution gives the judiciary the duty, not merely the power, to strike down any act tainted with grave abuse of discretion, defined as action contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence or done whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily. In AMARI, a unanimous Court through Justice Carpio held that reclaimed public land could be leased but not sold to a private corporation and submerged areas were inalienable, later finding a P140.16 billion price gap and calling the deal the grandmother of all scams. In PIATCO, written by Justice Puno, the Court found five defects, among them an award to a financially unqualified bidder, an amended agreement that destroyed the fair competition essence of bidding, prohibited government guarantees, and an exclusive Luzon terminal amounting to a monopoly. In MEGA PACIFIC, which he wrote, the contract went to an entity that had not bid, the machines flunked the DOST accuracy and audit-trail tests, the software could not prevent repeated downloads, and Comelec admitted testing only a demo version. He concluded that the Court had upheld the rule of law and the leveling of the playing field, advancing business in general even where particular contractors lost.
